Floating-Point Form of Numbers
  • In a floating-point system we write, for instance,
0.6247 · 103,0.1735 · 10−13,−0.2000 · 10−1, 6.247 · 102,1.735 · 10−14,−2.000 · 10−2.
Floating-Point Form
  • Fix the number of significant, whereas the decimal point is "floating."
  • A significant digit of a number c
    • except possibly for zeros to the left of the first nonzero digit; these zeros serve only to fix the position of the decimal point. (Thus any other zero is a significant digit of c)
13600,  1.3600,  0.0013600
  • In a text we indicate, say, 5 significant digits, by 5S.
Errors of Numeric Results
  • Final results of computations of unknown quantities generally are approximations.
    • Not exact but involve errors. Such an error may result from a combination of the following effects.
    • Roundoff errors result from rounding.
Taylor's Theorem
Suppose f ∈ Cn[a, b], that f(n + 1) exists on [a, b], and x0 ∈ [a, b]. For every x ∈ [a, b], there exists a number ξ(x) between x0 and x with
f(x) = Pn(x) + Rn(x),
where
Pn(x) = f(x0) + f′(x0)(x − x0) + f′′(x0)2! (x − x0)2 + ⋯ + f(n)(x0)n! (x − x0)n
= nk = 0 f(k)(x0)k! (x − x0)k
Experimental and Truncating Errors
  • Experimental errors are errors of given data (probably arising from measurements).
  • Truncating errors result from truncating (prematurely breaking off).
    • E.g., replace a Taylor series with the sum of its first few terms. These errors depend on the computational method used and must be dealt with individually for each method.

Finite Digit Arithmetic
Suppose that x = 57 and y = 13. Use five-digit chopping for calculating x + y, x − y, x × y, and x ÷ y.
Solution Note that
x = 57 = 0.714285  and  y = 13 = 0.3
implies that the five-digit chopping values of x and y are
fl(x) = 0.71428 × 100  and  fl(y) = 0.33333 × 100.
Thus
x + y= fl(fl(x) + fl(y)) = fl(0.71428 × 100 + 0.33333 × 100) = fl(1.04761 × 100) = 0.10476 × 101.
x =fl(x) =.× 1000
y =fl(y) =.× 1000
fl(x) + fl(y) =x + y =.× 100
Finite Digit Arithmetic
The true value is x + y = 57 + 13 = 2221, so we have
Absolute Error =2221 − 0.10476 × 101 = 0.190 × 10−4 Relative Error =0.190 × 10−422/21 = 0.182 × 10−4.

Algorithm
Algorithm
  • An unambiguous procedure
    • a finite sequence of steps in a specified order
  • Implement a procedure to solve a problem or
    approximate a solution to the problem.
  • Computational Thinking

Pseudocode
Form of the input to be supplied and the form of the desired output
The following algorithm computes x1 + x2 + ... + xN = ∑Ni=1 xi, given N and the numbers x1, x2, ..., xN.
INPUT N, x1, x2, ..., xN.
OUTPUT SUM = ∑Ni=1 xi.
Step 1Set SUM = 0.(Initialize accumulator.) Step 2For i = 1, 2, ..., N do set SUM = SUM + xi.(Add the next term.) Step 3OUTPUT(SUM); STOP.
Stopping Criterion
  • Not all numerical procedures give satisfactory output for arbitrarily chosen input.
  • Stopping technique independent of the numerical technique is incorporated into each algorithm to avoid infinite loop.
  • Example: Taylor series
  • Any idea?
Property of Algorithm
  • Stable: small changes in the initial data produce correspondingly small changes in the final results. An algorithm
  • Unstable and conditionally stable
  • linear error growth: En ≈ CnE0, C > 1
  • Exponential error growth: If En ≈ CnE0, for some
Error Growth
Solution of Equations by Iteration
Perhaps the easiest conceptual problem is to find solutions of a single equation
f(x) = 0,(1)
where f is a given function. A solution of (1) is a number x = s such that f(s) = 0.
Here, s suggests solution, but we shall also use other letters.
Fixed-Point Iteration for Solving Equations f(x) = 0
By some algebraic steps we transform (1) into the form
x = g(x).(2)
Then we choose an x0 and compute x1 = g(x0), x2 = g(x1), and in general
xn+1 = g(xn)  (n = 0, 1, ... ).(3)
A solution of (2) is called a fixed point of g, motivating the name of the method. This is a solution of (1), since from x = g(x) we can return to the original form f(x) = 0.
From (1) we may get several different forms of (2). The behavior of corresponding iterative sequences x0, x1, ... may differ, in particular, with respect to their speed of convergence. Indeed, some of them may not converge at all.
  • Up to the curve: height = g(x)
  • Across to the line y = x
  • That spot is the new x. Repeat.

Exercise 1
  • Find the Taylor Series for f(x) = ex about x = 0.
Exercise 2
  • Find the Taylor Series for f(x) = e−x about x = 0.
Exercise 3
  • Find the Taylor Series for f(x) = cos x about x = 0.
Exercise 4
  • Let p = 0.54617 and q = 0.54601. Use four-digit arithmetic to approximate p − q and determine the absolute and relative errors using (a) rounding and (b) chopping.
Exercise 5
  • Find the first approximate root of the equation 2x3 − 2x − 5 = 0 up to 4 decimal places.
Exercise 6
  • Find the first approximate root of the equation cos x = 3x − 1 up to 4 decimal places.
